s1: Hi, we're Paras and Harshita. This is The Echo Panel, our project for the Apart Research AI x Epistemics Sprint. More and more AI products answer a hard question with a panel: several models side by side, one model playing a set of experts, or agents that talk before they reply. When the panel agrees, it feels like corroboration. We asked a simple question. When five AI advisors agree, how many independent opinions did you actually get?
s2: Agreement is only evidence if the sources are independent. The philosopher Alvin Goldman made the point twenty-five years ago: a second expert who agrees adds evidence only if her view did not simply come from the first. Statistics says the same: dependent sources carry far less information, with a hard ceiling. And language models share training data, recipes and often the same documents. Meanwhile, people read AI consensus as social proof: in a recent study, a unanimous group of agents moved users' opinions faster and inflated their confidence.
s3: Here is the setup. We took 190 questions from ForecastBench, from Polymarket, Metaculus and Manifold, that resolved after every model's training cutoff. Each comes with the market's price, a human-crowd forecast the models never saw. Every panel has five advisors giving a probability and a one-line reason. We compare five designs: one model asked five times, five personas, five different models, the same five after one round of discussion, and after one shared brief. We measure independence the way a reader's inference needs it: how correlated the advisors are once you know the outcome. That gives an effective number of independent advisors, from five down to one.
s4: First result. One model asked five times is worth about 1.1 opinions. Giving those five calls expert personas, a political scientist, an economist, a superforecaster, adds almost nothing: 1.1 to 1.2. Five different OpenAI models do better, about 1.5. And when we crossed developers, OpenAI, Google, Alibaba and NVIDIA, it did not help: 1.41 against 1.42 on the same questions. The open-weight models from different companies were more alike than the OpenAI ones.
s5: Second result, and the one we did not expect to be this clean. We let the five models see each other's answers once and revise. Independence fell from 1.47 to 1.10, back to the level of a single model. The share of questions where all five agreed jumped from 56 to 84 percent. But unanimous panels were right 70 percent of the time before discussion and 68 percent after. Talking made them agree, not get it right. That is exactly what Lorenz and colleagues found in human groups in 2011. A shared brief was milder: slightly less independence, slightly better accuracy.
s6: Third result: what over-counting costs. If you read five agreeing advisors as five independent witnesses, the panels look 92 to 95 percent sure on average. They were right on 56 to 68 percent of questions. That reading worsens the Brier score by between 0.07 and 0.13, turning weak panels into harmful ones. For reference, the human prediction market scored 0.14 and beat every AI panel. Without web access the panels were close to the 0.25 you get by always saying fifty percent.
s7: Fourth result, and a surprise. We gave the same panels to two AI decision-makers and asked for a final forecast. Some got no note, some a generic warning, some a true independence label, these five carry about 1.5 opinions, and some a false label saying five. They simply averaged the panel, even when it was unanimous, and no note changed that. So machines average, and people count. The harm sits with human readers, which is where we think the label belongs.
s8: What should builders do? Show something closer to the effective number of advisors, because five on screen overstate the evidence three to five times. Don't present personas as independent experts. Collect answers before letting agents talk. And consider an independence label: one number from a panel's public track record that anyone can audit. A false label is just as easy to print, so who issues it matters. Our report includes a preregistered protocol for testing the label with people.
s9: To sum up. Five personas carry about one opinion. Five models, about one and a half. One round of discussion takes it back to one, while making the panel look far more certain. Reading agreement as corroboration costs real accuracy, and the people reading these panels are the ones at risk. The human study of the label is next. The report, code, every logged answer and an interactive replay are on our project page. Thank you.
